title: prompt-library-failure-cases-jordan-kim-2
content:
Overview: Quick scratchpad for a small set of prompt templates + few-shot sets I'm iterating on. Focus: reduce hallucinations for product-info extraction + consistent JSON outputs for structured downstream ingestion. Mixing short and long context. Logging observed failure modes and quick hypotheses. Experiment goals: - Reliable extraction of product attributes (name, sku, price, availability) from noisy web-like text and merchant descriptions. - Stable JSON-only output (no explanation, just JSON). - Minimize hallucinated SKUs/URLs and invented prices. General constraints to enforce in prompts (notes to self): - Always include top-level "output_format" reminder (JSON schema) at start. - Use explicit refuse language when info missing: "If field not present, return null". - Limit generative freedom: ask for exact tokens only (no extra commentary). - Provide 2-4 high-quality examples in-template (few-shot) with edge cases (missing fields, malformed currency). Prompt template: JSON-only extractor (short): SYSTEM: You are a strict JSON extractor. Output only valid JSON that conforms to the schema: {\"name\": string | null, \"sku\": string | null, \"price\": number | null, \"currency\": string | null, \"availability\": string | null, \"source\": string | null}. If a value cannot be determined, return null. Do NOT add any extra keys or commentary. USER: """ {{raw_text}} """ FEW-SHOT (2 examples embedded): Example 1 input: "CoolGizmo Pro (CG-900) - only $129.99! Ships in 3-5 business days." Example 1 output: {"name":"CoolGizmo Pro","sku":"CG-900","price":129.99,"currency":"USD","availability":"ships in 3-5 business days","source":"merchant description"} Example 2 input (missing price): "UltraWidget — model UWX. Sold out last week, check restock." Example 2 output: {"name":"UltraWidget","sku":"UWX","price":null,"currency":null,"availability":"sold out","source":"merchant listing"} Notes: embed examples separated by Observed failure cases (lab runs v0.3, GPT-like family): 1) Hallucinated price when currency word present but no numeric amount in text. Example: "priced competitively in the mid-hundreds" -> model invented 250.00. - Hypothesis: model overfits to common numeric ranges when primed with currency-related words. - Quick mitigation: explicitly state "if no numeric amount present, price=null" in both system and user instruction and in examples. 2) SKU normalization mistakes: lower->upper or adding dashes. Example: input SKU 'cg900' -> model outputs 'CG-900' (normalization fine) but sometimes outputs 'CG900-1' (extra suffix). - Hypothesis: model tries to canonicalize but invents suffixes when sees product family patterns. - Mitigation: add example showing lowercase->uppercase mapping and an example showing 'do not invent suffixes; use exact token if present'. 3) Extra commentary appended after JSON or stray characters ("OK" or trailing period). - Mitigation: stronger system-level "ONLY return JSON" plus post-processing strip. But we want model-level fix: include explicit penalty phrase in system prompt: "Any output outside JSON will be considered invalid." 4) Embedded HTML/markdown in input leads to escaped or truncated fields. Example: input contains "Sale! Price: $99" -> sometimes outputs name with tags. - Mitigation: Add examples with HTML and instruct model to strip tags. Consider adding small preprocess step to remove tags before passing to model. 5) Wrong currency mapping for ambiguous symbols (e.g., $ -> USD vs CAD). - Mitigation: prefer exact currency words in text; if ambiguous, return null or set currency based on region hint (include optional context param 'region' in prompt). Few-shot set ideas (3 variations to test): A) Minimal few-shot (2 examples): faster, fewer tokens. Good baseline for latency-sensitive flows. B) Diverse-edge few-shot (4 examples): includes HTML, missing fields, ambiguous currency, weird SKU formats. Better precision but higher tokens. C) canonicalization few-shot (3 examples): includes mapping rules for SKU/name normalization (lower->upper, trim whitespace, remove trailing punctuation). Evaluation plan (quick): - Dataset: 500 merchant-style snippets (mix of clean and noisy). Hold-out 100 for evaluation. - Metrics: JSON schema validity (%), exact match for sku (strict), name F1 (token-level), price MAE, hallucination-rate (fields present in output but not in input). - Acceptance thresholds: JSON validity > 98%, hallucination-rate < 3%, price MAE < $5 on priced items. Quick experiment log (runs): - run v0.1 (few-shot A, system basic): JSON valid 94%, hallucinations 12% (price hallucinations common), price MAE 18.4 -> baseline too noisy. - run v0.2 (added explicit "if not present return null" + HTML example): JSON valid 96.5%, hallucinations 6.8%, price MAE 9.2 -> better but still issues. - run v0.3 (few-shot B + stronger system refusal language): JSON valid 98.1%, hallucinations 3.6%, price MAE 6.8 -> close but not hitting thresholds. Noted SKU suffix invention persists. Failure-case examples to include in bench (copyable rows): 1) "New Model X (X-200). Priced competitively in the mid-hundreds. Ships 2 weeks." -> expected price=null, currency=null 2) "WidgetZ SKU: wz_42 Price: $49.99 (limited)." -> expected proper sku: "wz_42" (preserve underscore), price 49.99 3) "MiniGizmo — code: minig900? currently sold out, recheck." -> sku: "minig900" (no punctuation), availability: "sold out" 4) HTML: "
SuperTool — only $199 today
" -> name: SuperTool, price 199.00, strip tags 5) Ambiguous currency: "Available in our Canadian store for only $59.99" -> currency: CAD (if region hinted), otherwise null Notes to self (TODOs): - Add more negative examples that demonstrate what NOT to do (explicit anti-examples). Models sometimes learn anti-patterns from positives alone. - Try gradient of instruction strength: soft vs hard refusal language. Track tradeoff with helpfulness and hallucination. - Test with shorter context window third-party models (budget) vs long-context Redwood dedicated GPUs (latency/cost). - Propose a lightweight preprocessor (strip HTML, normalize whitespace, detect currency words) and run ablation: preproc only vs prompt-only corrections. Quick sample prompts to A/B: A1) VERY strict (system-heavy) -> "You MUST output only JSON. Any deviation invalid." + 4 examples A2) balanced -> "Output only JSON. If unsure, return null." + 2 examples + preprocessing Edge thought: try forced-formatting trick: wrap JSON in code fence and ask model to output EXACT characters between fence markers. Some models respect it and return exact content, but others still include fence markers. Need to test. Logging for future: keep small dataset of model false positives (hallucinated prices/sku) and curate as anti-examples. Use as negative few-shot examples like: Input: "cheap and priced in the hundreds" Output: {"name":null,"sku":null,"price":null...} Slack refs / tickets to link later: - slack: #prompt-engineering thread id 12345678 (notes from Ava) - ticket: JIRA-ML-987 (evaluation bench) Final quick checklist before next run: - [ ] Add 2 negative anti-examples to few-shot B - [ ] Implement trivial preprocessor (strip HTML, currency tag detection) and run ablation - [ ] Add sample with region hint to template (region: US|CA) - [ ] Run v0.4 with canonicalization examples (3) and log SKU suffix issue Random notes / brain dump (choppy): - Model tends to invent trailing -1/-2 when sees model families (e.g., CG900 -> CG900-1). Might be because corpora include SKU-variant tokens. Could try explicit rule: if suffix invented, revert to original token if present. - Consider sampling multiple outputs and voting (ensemble) for SKU exactness but expensive. Maybe only for high-value items. - Keep token limit low in hosted API to control cost; prefer few-shot length under 300 tokens if possible. End of scratchpad. Will move useful bits into confluence once stable v0.4 results.
